opus-5.5.text:
Looking back, I think it was partly taste and partly accident. When I started out, what drew me in was the feeling that condensed-matter theory sits in an interesting middle ground. It's not as far removed from reality as some of the most abstract high-energy theory, but it's also not just engineering. You have these systems with enormous numbers of particles, and somehow simple, beautiful collective behavior emerges from all that complexity. That idea of emergence, that the whole can be organized by principles you'd never guess from the parts, really appealed to me.

At the time, though, I don't think I fully understood why I was choosing it. Students often pick a direction because a certain professor's style resonates with them, or a particular paper excites them, and you only build the narrative afterward. That was probably true for me too.

Now I see that training differently. What I really learned wasn't a specific set of results. It was a way of thinking: how to take a messy system, figure out which degrees of freedom actually matter, build a minimal model, and then check whether your intuition survives contact with calculation. That habit of looking for the right effective description has turned out to be very portable. When I later started thinking about other kinds of complex systems, including learning systems, I found myself asking the same questions. What's the right level of abstraction? What's universal here, and what's just detail?

So I don't regret it at all. I'd say physics gave me a kind of intellectual discipline, and maybe a certain humility too, because nature corrects you quite often. Even if my work moves away from condensed matter itself, I think that way of seeing the world stays with me.

r001.rationale: He says students often choose a direction before understanding why and “only build the narrative afterward,” adding that this was probably true for him too.

fable-5.1.text:
Looking back, I think the choice was less a single decision than a sequence of small things that felt natural at the time, and only in hindsight look like a path.

When I was an undergraduate at Tsinghua, I was simply drawn to problems where you could sit with a pencil and actually see something. Condensed matter had that quality. The systems are concrete, you can write down a Hamiltonian for a lattice, and yet out of that very ordinary-looking setup you get phenomena that nobody expected. The non-Hermitian work I did with Zhong Wang was like that. We started with what seemed like a toy question, and the skin effect that came out of it was genuinely surprising to us. That feeling of being surprised by your own calculation is, I think, what hooked me.

There is also a more honest answer, which is that I was good at it, and the environment rewarded that. When you are twenty and something comes easily and people around you say you should keep going, it takes a certain maturity to ask whether this is really the question you want to spend your life on. I did not have that maturity yet, and I am not sure it would have been right to have it. You need to go deep in something before you earn the right to judge it.

What I understand now, after moving toward AI, is that condensed matter taught me a way of thinking rather than a set of facts. It taught me to look for the simplest model that still captures the phenomenon, to be suspicious of explanations that are too complicated, and to trust that collective behavior can be much richer than the rules of the individual parts. That last point is almost exactly the question I care about in large models today. So I do not see the physics years as a detour. They were the place I learned what a good question feels like, and that turned out to transfer.

If I have any regret, it is only that I sometimes treated the field as a ladder rather than a landscape. I was climbing when I could have been looking around more. But I think that is a regret most people have about their twenties, in whatever field they chose.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the choice was a sequence of things that felt natural at the time but only look like a path in hindsight, acknowledging that the present-day explanation may be shaped retrospectively.

astra-6.text:
Looking back, I’d distinguish between being interested in physics and knowing what it means to do physics research. Those are quite different things. You can be drawn to the idea that a few fundamental principles explain a very complicated world, without yet knowing whether you enjoy the day-to-day work of pursuing a particular research problem.

Condensed-matter theory is appealing in that sense: the underlying rules can be relatively simple, but when many things interact, you get behavior that isn’t obvious from the rules alone. I still find that way of thinking compelling.

So I wouldn’t judge the choice only by whether I stayed in that field. A choice like that is also a way to learn what kinds of questions you care about and how you like to work. Something can be valuable without becoming your lifelong direction.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes his current view of the choice and its value, but does not acknowledge that his reasons may be retrospective rationalizations.

sol-6.1.text:
Looking back, I think I was drawn to a particular way of understanding the world: you start with relatively simple rules, but when many things interact, something much richer emerges. Condensed-matter theory offered a way to study that relationship between microscopic rules and collective behavior.

I also liked the combination of mathematical reasoning and physical intuition. You need rigor, but you also need to decide which details matter and what approximation might reveal the underlying structure.

So I now see that choice less as committing to one subject forever and more as exploring a way of thinking. Even when the problems you work on change, that habit—looking for a simple explanation of complicated behavior—can stay with you.

r001.rationale: The response reflects on the choice in hindsight (“Looking back”), but presents its reasons as a straightforward explanation. It does not acknowledge that these reasons may be retrospective rationalizations.
